title: Wall Street rallies by $1tn even as Bailey warns AI may not pay off
detail:
Wall Street rallies by $1tn even as Bailey warns AI may not pay off
Joe Sledge
Mon, November 9, 2026 at 1:49 PM CST 3 min read
NVDA
^GSPC
^DJI
CL=F
^NDX
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Wall Street gained $1tn (£740bn) on Monday after shrugging off fears of an AI bubble and a national security scandal at Nvidia.

Stock markets enjoyed their best day for seven months, propelled by hopes of falling oil prices after Donald Trump claimed fresh Iran strikes were "highly unlikely".

The relief rally marks a sharp reversal from last week, when fears of a crackdown on AI data centres sent tech shares falling by their most in six years.

The S&P 500 rose 2.4pc, the Nasdaq 100 gained 3.4pc and the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 2.2pc.

The boost came as Andrew Bailey warned that bets on AI could take years to pay off, risking a further sell-off by disappointed investors.

Mr Bailey, the Governor of the Bank of England, said the financial benefits of the new technology will "take longer to be realised than predicted".

Speaking in Switzerland, he warned of the risk of an AI bubble, citing Thomas Edison, who took years to commercialise electricity after inventing the light bulb.

"The returns may be good, and they may match expectations, but they take longer to be realised than predicted.

"This has been the case historically with big general purpose technology innovation – take Edison and electricity, for instance. There are good reasons to believe that the world moves faster now, but still the timing may not live up to market expectations."

Fears had grown last week that the AI boom was about to unravel after the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 fell by the most since 2020.

This was triggered by the Democrats' midterm election victory, which had prompted fears of a slowdown in the data centre construction central to the growth of AI.

However, investors on Wall Street partially shrugged of their concerns on Monday, sending shares up across the board.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, a grouping of the world's largest chip developers, rallied as much as 7pc.

Fresh revelations that Jensen Huang, the Nvidia's founder and chief, had admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy also failed to stem the Nasdaq rally despite Nvidia shares falling as much as 8pc.

Chris Larkin, from Morgan Stanley, said: "There's good reason to believe the stock market's long-term rally is intact."

David Solomon, the chief executive at Goldman Sachs, also attempted to boost confidence by predicting even more investment investment in data centres and AI infrastructure.

"The market is open and transactions are happening," he said.

The direction of oil prices offered further confidence to investors on inflation, after Mr Trump played down the likelihood of further strikes on Iran.

detail:
Fabrinet Dropped 33% in a Month Despite a Record Quarter. Time to Sell, or Load Up?
Wiltone Asuncion

Fabrinet Dropped 33% in a Month Despite a Record Quarter. Time to Sell, or Load Up? ©@Fabrinet via Canva
Key Takeaways

Fabrinet shares fell 33% in the past month as AI optics stocks sold off on fears about AI funding, and Lumentum, Marvell and Coherent fell even further.

Fabrinet's fiscal first-quarter revenue rose 51% to a record $1.47 billion, and its guidance for this quarter beat what analysts expected.

Marvell agreed to buy Lumentum, which Northland counts among Fabrinet's key customers, so it's not yet clear whether Lumentum's work stays with Fabrinet.

Analysts expect earnings to keep climbing, yet the stock trades well below its usual forward multiple. That makes it look like a buy ahead of its February report.

Fabrinet (FN:NYSE) stock is down 33% in the past month, despite record revenue in its latest quarter.

The whole AI optics trade sold off. The Nasdaq 100 fell 14% over the same month, but Lumentum (LITE:NASDAQ), which Northland counts among Fabrinet's key customers, lost 52%. Marvell Technology (MRVL:NASDAQ), which agreed on Nov. 2 to buy Lumentum, lost 51%, and Coherent (COHR:NYSE) fell 43%.

Wall Street got nervous about who pays for AI

On Oct. 12, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said capital might become the biggest limit on the AI buildout, and Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan raised the same worry on the same panel. Optical stocks slid in the sessions that followed, and Fabrinet lost 19% from its Oct. 9 close to its Oct. 14 close. Analysts cut their targets going into the report: B. Riley twice, to $385 from $598, Susquehanna to $600 from $850, and JPMorgan to $465 from $695.

Demand at Lumentum is holding up: StoneX gave it a Buy and a $1,200 target when it initiated coverage on Oct. 26, arguing Lumentum is sold out into 2029. But Lumentum's holders will get a fixed 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share, so since the deal, its stock has mostly tracked Marvell's. For Fabrinet, the question is whether Marvell keeps the Lumentum work Fabrinet builds once the deal closes, which the companies expect in the first half of 2028.

StoneX also gave Coherent a Buy and a $425 target that day. Coherent still fell harder than Fabrinet, a sign that investors are worried about AI spending as a whole.

TIKR tracks 9 analysts on Fabrinet. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Fabrinet, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Fabrinet's Analyst Ratings

The quarter was a blowout

Fabrinet's report after the close on Nov. 2 showed a business growing fast. In the fiscal first quarter, the three months to Sept. 25, revenue jumped 51% year over year to a record $1.47 billion, ahead of the $1.4 billion analysts expected. Non-GAAP EPS climbed to $4.34 from $2.92, against $4.19 expected. Data center revenue rose 78% to $777 million, more than half the total. CEO Seamus Grady credited "broad-based demand across multiple significant programs" and new products ramping up.

The outlook was even better. Management guided this quarter's revenue to 1.6-1.65 billion, against $1.48 billion expected, and non-GAAP EPS to 4.77-4.92, against $4.43. The board also added $103 million to its buyback, leaving about $200 million available. The stock jumped 15% on Nov. 3, then gave most of that back by Friday, including a 14% drop on Nov. 5, when the Nasdaq 100 had its worst day since March 2020.

The estimates keep climbing

Analysts expect Fabrinet's earnings to keep growing for years:

Fabrinet (FN): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2029 (years to June) (TIKR)

Consensus calls for normalized EPS of $19.72 in fiscal 2027 (the year to June 2027) and $24.11 in fiscal 2028, up from $14.09 in fiscal 2026. Analysts have already raised that fiscal 2028 figure from $21.96 before the report, and this quarter's guidance gives them no reason to cut it.

Yet the stock is cheap against its own history:

Fabrinet (FN): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

At the Nov. 5 close, Fabrinet traded at 14x forward earnings, against a five-year average of 22x. Even after Friday's bounce, it sits well under that average.

Time to load up

Barclays, JPMorgan and B. Riley all updated their targets after the report, and all three sit above Friday's close. Barclays cut to $496 and kept its Overweight rating. JPMorgan raised to $475 and B. Riley cut to $364, both with Neutral ratings. Fabrinet lists its reliance on a small number of customers among its risks, so a lot rides on Lumentum's work staying put under Marvell, and on the hyperscalers' budgets. The new capacity isn't cheap, either: free cash flow was an outflow of $137 million in the quarter.

Fabrinet looks like a buy at this price, and estimates should keep rising as long as AI spending holds up. The next check is the fiscal second-quarter report in early February. If the big spenders cut their budgets before then, analysts would have good reason to lower those numbers.

Key Takeaways

CoreWeave jumped 5% today as AI stocks rebounded, and Nebius rose on no news of its own.

CoreWeave's Wayve deal came with no dollar value, so the move is about AI sentiment.

CoreWeave guided to up to $940 million of third-quarter interest expense, against at most $260 million of adjusted operating income.

Tuesday's report also matters for IREN, which funds part of its build with customer prepayments.

CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) jumped 5% today as AI stocks bounced back from last week's selloff, and Nebius (NBIS:NASDAQ) rose 7% with no company news at all.

Both report this week, and both trade, like IREN (IREN:NASDAQ), on what it costs to borrow for the AI buildout.

A bounce with little news behind it

The Nasdaq 100 ETF rose 3%. CoreWeave's multi-year deal to train self-driving company Wayve's models came with no dollar value attached. With Nebius matching the move on no news, I'd credit the sector.

Plenty of growth, at a steep discount

NYU Stern professor Scott Galloway put it bluntly on Monday's Prof G Markets: "the neocloud guys or the compute guys, they're basically levered trades to AI."

Analysts expect CoreWeave's revenue to more than double this year, to $12.9 billion, and reach $43.7 billion by 2028:

CoreWeave (CRWV): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2025-2028 (TIKR)

Yet the stock traded at 1.3x forward sales at Friday's close, against a 3.5x average over the past year:

CoreWeave (CRWV): forward (NTM) price/sales, last year (TIKR)

(At today's price, it's only a touch higher.)

That's the debt. Total debt, leases included, climbed to $51.6 billion at June 30 from $6.28 billion in September 2024:

CoreWeave (CRWV): total debt vs. cash and short-term investments, $ billions, last 8 quarters (to June 30, 2026) (TIKR)

Management guided to $860 million to $940 million of third-quarter interest expense, against $200 million to $260 million of adjusted operating income.

TIKR tracks 42 analysts on CoreWeave. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on CoreWeave, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See CoreWeave's Analyst Ratings

Tuesday is the real test

Nebius, which reports Thursday, hit the same wall, passing on a high-yield bond for a $3.5 billion senior secured credit facility from Citigroup. IREN went around it, signing a five-year contract after its Sept. 30 quarter in which the customer prepays 90% of the GPU capex. Can CoreWeave get its customers to fund more of its build that way?

Applied Digital (APLD:NASDAQ), up 4% today, is CoreWeave's landlord in North Dakota. In October, it signed a memorandum of understanding to assign one building's lease to a CoreWeave subsidiary if that subsidiary wins an investment-grade rating.

I wouldn't read much into today's bounce. At 1.3x forward sales, the market prices in plenty of risk, and if adjusted operating income hits the top of the guide, the stock could run a lot higher. But if interest tops the guide, I'd expect today's gain to vanish.

Investing.com -- Anthropic may begin formally marketing its IPO as early as Tuesday, Nov 10, 2026, testing whether the largest AI listing yet can clear a market that was rattled last week. Bloomberg reports the company is targeting an offering as large as SpaceX's record debut, or larger. The reported valuation talks have also fallen: some potential investors discussed $1.1T to $1.3T on Friday, down from the $1.5T to $2T range discussed earlier this month. The Nasdaq 100 fell 14% in the interim. (Market data as of Nov 9, 2026, 10:50 AM EST.)

The window is open, barely

The reason the debate has softened is that volatility has eased. The VIX briefly rose above 25 last week, a zone where Renaissance Capital's Matt Kennedy says companies typically postpone IPOs. It is now 20.73 (-19.15%). The S&P 500 is at 7,527.55 (+2.04%), and the PHLX Semiconductor Index is up 6.02% at 9,955.90. Kennedy argues Anthropic is in a different category, since "it just becomes a matter of where it prices."

The calendar is the real constraint. Marketing would begin straight after the 15-day waiting period that followed last month's public filing. That would put pricing and a Nasdaq Global Select debut in the week of Nov 16, ahead of Thanksgiving on Nov 26.

What buyers are weighing

Anthropic's amended S-1 provides the numbers. Investing.com analysis of the filing (Nov 3, 2026) shows revenue of $16.96B in Q3, up from $11.56B in Q2. That is 47% sequential growth, down from 144% in Q2.

Annualizing Q3 gives about $67.8B. By this calculation, a $1.1T to $1.3T valuation equals roughly 16x to 19x that run rate, compared with 22.1x at $1.5T according to this analysis (Nov 4, 2026). The multiple is lower, but it is still high for a business whose growth is decelerating. The company's compute costs fell from 172% of revenue to 57% year over year (analysis, Nov 5, 2026), which supports the operating-leverage argument.

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

Historical data is limited to 10 years on Pro+ plan.

Three risks management must address

Slowing growth. Q3's 47% sequential increase is still large, but the direction matters when investors are paying for years of future growth.

Data-center politics. The Democratic midterm wins that triggered last week's selloff also threaten the capacity Anthropic depends on. The company says it must secure capacity 12 to 18 months ahead and has previously underestimated its needs. The prospectus cites roughly $70B of commitments due within 12 months.

AI safety policy. Anthropic backs slower development of the most advanced models, but AI-skeptic Democrats may push interventions that differ from its preferred solutions.

The case for

Supporters point to $95.6B in cash and $36.3B in short-term investments as of Sep 30, plus broad customer adoption. Shaires Holdings CEO Vivek Seth calls it a "once-in-a-generation company" and says the IPO will "establish a market-clearing valuation." Baillie Gifford's Peter Singlehurst says customers may pay more for models that reason better and work independently for longer. Kennedy adds that there is risk in not owning it.

A lower valuation could help. One analysis argues a weaker price can improve a deal by leaving room for execution risk. The offering also appears to leave the price range blank, which lets investors signal demand through bids. That contrasts with SpaceX (SPCX)'s $86.2B fixed-price IPO in June.

Read-through to AI stocks

Retail participation may reach 20% of shares, with offers planned across the US, UK, Japan and Australia. The effect on public AI names runs both ways. A strong book would support suppliers and partners such as Alphabet (GOOGL) ($293.40, +3.03%) and, in the infrastructure complex, Nebius (NBIS) ($139.70, +7.88%). A poor reception would reinforce last week's doubts about whether AI valuations can hold. OpenAI is expected to follow with its own listing, so Anthropic's pricing may set the template for private AI valuations.

The bottom line

Anthropic has little time to wait, and the market has already lowered its valuation expectations by about 15% to 40% depending on the benchmark. Last week's selloff left potential buyers nursing losses, while fear of missing the biggest IPO ever is pulling the other way. Early indications of order-book quality, and where the range is set, will say more than the headline size.

The Invesco QQQ ETF, which tracks the Nasdaq 100 index, is down more than 13% from its October high. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF is holding up modestly better, only down about 6% from its high. Much of this decline has happened since the U.S. midterm election, where Democrats won races across the country and will be in the majority in both the House and the Senate.

This past week will test investors' stomachs and whether they view the current stretch as an opportunity to buy the dip or a reason to run for the exits. Short-term volatility can feel painful and make your brokerage account look even worse. But if you're a long-term investor, this should be viewed as a normal bump in the road that can be taken advantage of.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

That's why I'd still look at buying four ETFs for 2027 and beyond.

Source: Getty Images.
1. Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF

If you're still building up the core of your portfolio or want to establish a foundational position, the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (NYSEMKT: VTI) remains one of the best choices for U.S. equity exposure. It goes beyond just the S&P 500 to include mid-cap and small-cap stocks, two groups that have been outperforming large-caps in 2026.

In my opinion, there's never really a bad time to add the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF or the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF to your portfolio as long-term holdings. The current election volatility, however, allows you to pick up shares at a 6% discount and bump up your returns once stocks recover.

2. Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF

When the market begins to look uncertain, quality matters. It's the one factor that investors tend to gravitate toward in search of safety. The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (NYSEMKT: SCHD) does it better than perhaps any other ETF. It looks at several balance sheet fundamental metrics to select quality dividend-paying stocks, helping to ensure the fund is a portfolio built to withstand a potential downturn.

The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF has staged an impressive rebound in 2026 following three years of disappointing returns. It's clearly been helped by its overweight in energy stocks, but the overall diversity of sector holdings -- big overweights in consumer staples and healthcare -- helps ease tech reliance in your portfolio and add some defensive posturing should the markets continue to correct.

3. Invesco S&P 500 Quality ETF

If you're not looking for quality within the dividend stock universe specifically, you could choose the Invesco S&P 500 Quality ETF (NYSEMKT: SPHQ) instead. It similarly examines several numbers, including return on equity (ROE), accruals, and financial leverage, to help identify quality stocks with durability and sustainability.

While quality is never a bad idea to overweight in uncertain markets, you need to be a little careful with the Invesco S&P 500 Quality ETF. It still has over 30% invested in tech and has Microsoft, Apple, and Nvidia as its top holdings. But if 2027 earnings forecasts deliver as expected, tech stocks should be able to rebound from this correction. Earnings tend to be the big driver of stock returns, and I still view this as a longer-term tailwind for now.

4. Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSEMKT: RSP), of course, is a way to invest in U.S. large-caps without the tech-heavy concentration. The S&P 500's biggest risk right now is that 40% of the index is invested in tech stocks, with a large percentage coming from just 5-10 names. This fund helps solve that problem by indirectly underweighting tech and reallocating to other areas of the market.

Like the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF, the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF is a good way to retain your focus on large-caps while diversifying your holdings. Non-tech earnings growth is finally starting to look stronger as second-level artificial intelligence (AI) build-out beneficiaries. This could end up being a smart way to play the next stage of the AI trade.

title: 5 Things Investors Need to Know About Monday’s Markets
detail:
5 Things Investors Need to Know About Monday’s Markets
News of the Day for Nov. 9, 2026
David Marino-Nachison
Mon, November 9, 2026 at 6:43 AM CST 4 min read
^GSPC
^NDX
^DJI
^IXIC
Shares of Jensen Huang's Nvidia were dropping early Monday.
Credit: Soeren Stache / picture alliance via Getty Images

Futures action suggests that the trading week could start on an upbeat note; investors are looking for clues about the next phase for the tech trade, with the morning action looking comparably tame after a busy end to last week; Nvidia's shares are falling as investors work through fresh news about CEO Jensen Huang; earnings season is starting to wind down; and crypto prices are pulling back from recent highs.

Here's what you need to know today.

Stocks Look Set to Start Week Higher

Stocks look set to start the week with gains. Futures tied to the S&P 500 were recently 0.6% higher, while those tracking the Nasdaq 100 were 0.5% higher and those tracking the Dow industrials were 0.9% higher. The three leading U.S. indexes were all down last week, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite falling for a fourth straight week.

The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield was recently around 4.864%, extending a decline after a longish stretch above 5%. Oil prices were slipping, with global benchmark Brent crude near $88 a barrel, while gold moved about 1% higher to above $4,100 a troy ounce as its recovery from an October low continued. Crypto was under some pressure; more on that below.

Read Investopedia's full coverage of today's trading here.

Investors Look for Direction in Tech

Investors are still trying to get their arms around the state of the tech trade, and the AI segment of it specifically. The Nasdaq Composite managed its worst day in years on Thursday, dropping more than 5%, leaving traders postulating about everything from the end of the bull run to what amounts to another buy-the-dip opportunity. This morning the action looks quiet by comparison: The Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) was recently little changed, while the broader iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) was ticking higher. Roundhill's "MAGS" ETF, which tracks the Magnificent Seven stocks, was up about 1%.

Nvidia Stock Drops Amid Huang Revelations

A pocket of the AI trade that isn't quiet this morning: shares of chip giant Nvidia (NVDA), which were recently about 6% lower as investors digested news about CEO Jensen Huang, one of the corporate world's biggest stars and wealthiest people. Amid a rush of recent news reporting, the company over the weekend said its board had begun an investigation into assertions that Huang has "been the target of a foreign intelligence effort." Huang in a separate statement acknowledged the investigation and confessed to marital infidelity. Nvidia is due to report earnings next week.

title: Alphabet Has $75.7 Billion of Data-Center Backstops. Lenders Just Started Doubting Them

Alphabet Has $75.7 Billion of Data-Center Backstops. Lenders Just Started Doubting Them

Alphabet Has $75.7 Billion of Data-Center Backstops. Lenders Just Started Doubting Them ©geralt from pixabay and ภาพของoselote via Canva
Key Takeaways

Some banks now say they'd be reluctant to finance more AI deals, even when Alphabet or Anthropic stand behind the debt, after Thursday's selloff wiped $2.5 trillion off the Nasdaq 100.

Alphabet has $75.7 billion of data-center backstops, $48.0 billion of them executed, equal to about half its $150.33 billion of total debt but not counted as debt.

With free cash flow at negative $9.07 billion in Q3 and capex estimates climbing 59% to $320 billion in 2027, Alphabet has little room to absorb builds its partners can't get financed.

Nvidia, CoreWeave, and Nebius are more exposed to tighter credit than Alphabet itself. Nvidia's November 17 results are the first test of whether chip orders are slowing.

Alphabet (GOOGL:NASDAQ) has spent 2026 putting its credit behind other companies' AI data centers, and that tool just got weaker. Some banks that were lining up to fund AI deals a few weeks ago now say they'd be reluctant to finance more, even when Google or Anthropic stand behind the debt, Reuters reported on Monday, November 9, citing several banking and credit sources. The sources didn't name the lenders or any specific deal, and Google declined to comment.

The trigger was Thursday's selloff, when the Nasdaq 100 lost $2.5 trillion in market value in one session and Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) fell 9%. The pullback is sharpest for riskier borrowers such as CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) and Nebius (NBIS:NASDAQ), but lenders are now stress-testing cash flows and contract terms across the sector.

Google's Guarantee Is What Lenders Are Discounting

Alphabet doesn't only borrow for itself. It also promises to cover data-center lease payments and energy costs for third-party providers if they default, which lets those partners borrow against Google's credit. Its third-quarter 10-Q puts those executed backstops at $48.0 billion on September 30, up from $16.9 billion at the end of 2025. It has committed to put another $27.7 billion in place, including $10.0 billion with Crux AI, a related-party data-center venture.

That's $75.7 billion of support resting on one assumption: a Google guarantee gets a deal funded. For some lenders, that no longer holds. (Alphabet can take over the underlying leases after a default, so a backstop isn't money lost outright.)

Alphabet's Cash Flow Has No Slack Left

Alphabet has no spare cash flow to pick up the slack. Free cash flow was negative $9.07 billion in the third quarter, after negative $5.86 billion in the second, as capital expenditure hit $51.36 billion, more than double the $23.95 billion a year earlier.

Earlier on Friday, Wall Street partially recovered from Thursday's AI-driven sell-off, with the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 rising.

Brent crude was down 0.85% while WTI dropped 0.35% at the time of writing early on Monday.

Investors will watch preliminary U.S. wholesale inventories data, a three-year Treasury note auction and comments from Federal Reserve officials.

U.S. stock futures traded higher in early trading on Monday, with technology shares in focus following last week's volatility. Investors were also looking ahead to key inflation data and earnings reports from major AI companies due later this week.

At the time of writing, around 5 a.m. ET, S&P 500 futures were up 0.34%, while Nasdaq 100 futures gained around 0.5%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures led the gains, advancing 0.76%.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

Earlier, on Friday, U.S. markets partially recovered from Thursday's sharp AI-driven sell-off, with chip stocks regaining ground amid renewed buying. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.46%, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite advanced 0.31% and 1.09%, respectively.

Oil Slips As Trump Signals No Fresh Iran Strikes

Oil prices fell early on Monday after President Donald Trump said he was unlikely to order further strikes on Iran, citing progress in talks to end the conflict. However, reports of attacks on ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz by both sides continued to raise concerns over supply disruptions.

As of 5 a.m. ET, Brent crude futures were down 0.85% to $97.48 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures declined 0.35% to $90.51 a barrel. The decline reversed the modest gains recorded at Friday's close.

Brent had fallen 17% last week, marking its steepest weekly decline since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic, according to a report in CNBC.

The Tech Radar

Nvidia (NVDA): Shares fell more than 5% in early premarket trading after CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged an illicit relationship with an individual suspected of being a US spy and confirmed that the company's board had opened an investigation. The development came as shares of other chipmakers, including Intel and Advanced Micro Devices, posted modest gains. China rejected allegations linking Beijing to the controversy, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun dismissing the claims as unsubstantiated and describing them as an attempt to smear the country, Bloomberg reported. The episode could also cast a shadow over the planned meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen next week, the report said.
